item.title: The Perils of Perfectionism
item.description:
Perfectionism

The Perils of Perfectionism

Letting go of perfectionism means you are honoring your human limits.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Perfectionism is driven by a compulsive need, not genuine self-improvement.
  • Striving for perfection can isolate us emotionally and disconnect us from others.
  • There’s no final “arrival”—perfection is unattainable, and that's deeply human.
Source: Luis Villasmil/Unsplash

We can understand perfectionism as an attachment and a striving to be perfect. Perfectionism goes beyond endeavoring to improve. It’s driven by a compulsive need to improve and by the illusion that we can reach a flawless state of being. I mentioned to a colleague that it seems increasingly popular to believe that one’s "arrival" is imminent. He responded, “Oh no, it’s been popular for several thousand years.” Hard work and a measure of good luck may contribute to our achievements being noteworthy. However, such success does not exempt us from being imperfect.

What’s the Draw?

We seem to be easily drawn to perfectionism. We even enjoy using the word perfect in casual conversation. A waiter in a restaurant says, “Perfect!” after taking my order. Thankfully, I remember that my veggie burger, accompanied by sweet potato fries, will not transcend human, culinary conditions. Let’s look at some of the reasons behind our fascination with the dynamic of perfection.

  • We achieve an impervious state of personal worth.
  • We are insulated from judgments of being lethargic or lacking ambition.
  • The busyness of striving distracts from feeling vulnerable or fragile.
  • The shine of improvement will likely yield the respect and admiration of others.
  • Our improvements might finally get the benevolent attention of our parents.

What’s the Cost?

  • The overriding cost is that an attachment to perfectionism is an assault upon our humanity.
  • Compulsively striving compromises a capacity to be present. Perfectionism keeps us on task with myopic vision. We easily lose sight of what is actually happening around us, especially as we relate to others.
  • We are condemned to proving we’re OK. Settling into simply feeling good about ourselves fades as we remain focused on the next best demonstration of our worth.
  • We become driven by heroic aspirations. Perfectionism is typically driven by a hero’s persona. As such, limits are denied, personal needs are neglected, and self-care is ignored. Hence, the following from the author F. Scott Fitzgerald: “Show me a hero and I’ll write you a tragedy.”
  • We are subject to emotional isolation. A preoccupation with attaining perfection will insulate us from others who are likely up to the business of being ordinary people.
  • We pretend there’s an "arrival." It’s too easy to believe that all the hard work of perfectionism must lead to the arrival of some flawless state. Hence, the distortion of believing you have arrived becomes extremely seductive.

Bring Care to Perfectionism

When success accompanies being perfectionistic, it becomes more seductive to remain a perfectionist, ignoring the non-perfectionistic nature of our humanity. Here are some suggestions for supporting your perfectionism.

  • Notice and appreciate your ability to work hard.
  • Become aware of how demanding you are of yourself, and the possible losses involved when you’re that demanding. Common losses include sleep, exercise, healthy eating, dental and medical care, friendships, family connections, and time for fun and enjoyment.
  • Take time to grieve your losses.
  • Shift your attitude toward work from a place where you prove something to a place where you love something.
  • Learn to view perfectionism as a form of compensation. Compulsively doing too much often reflects not caring enough for yourself, compensating for the diminished care.
  • Accept that there’s no "arrival." You don’t arrive at a perfected state. You remain a non-perfect human being. Whenever possible, associate with others who have let go of their perfectionistic tendencies and celebrate life together.

There are benefits to choosing to be an ordinary, non-perfect person. Projects and tasks can feel easier and more graceful, since they don't determine our personal worth. People find us more approachable when our energies aren't in high gear. There’s the ability to live with a light heart. Such a heart lives close to joy, curiosity, awe, and wonder.

item.title: Living With Parents as a Young Adult: The Unexpected Bonus
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Living With Parents as a Young Adult: The Unexpected Bonus

How boomeranging changes old parent-child patterns into desirable camaraderie.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Parents who accept their children as adults have an easier time relearning to live with them.
  • The stigma of adult children moving back home has faded, enabling closer family bonds.
  • Living together as adults can elevate the old parent-child relationship to friendship status.
Source: Erda Estremera/Unsplash

The pandemic brought young adults home to parents—millions of them. Some stayed, while many forged out on their own when it was safe to do so. Once again, the number of young adults between the ages of 24 and 35 returning to their childhood bedrooms is growing. Currently, the migration home is most noticeable among recent college grads who are having difficulty finding jobs they love or are trained for and affording rent to live independently.

Deciding to Live at Home Again

The social stigma of returning home that plagued earlier generations of young adults has disappeared. A return to the nest now is more about being willing to work out any lingering kinks and everyone feeling comfortable with the redefined relationship.

During the research for my book Under One Roof Again: All Grown Up and (Re)learning to Live Together Happily, almost every parent I spoke with said they were delighted to be living with their adult child again. The business of growing up leaves little time to spend together. A return home gives you that time to talk, to get a better understanding of who you are as an individual and not necessarily a clone of a parent.

Young adults have the opportunity to see their parents as people, not solely mom and dad who set the boundaries and enforced the rules. The insights that come from sharing space as grown-ups go a long way toward creating harmony.

Whether parent and child are together for the long or short haul, the willingness to bend when necessary, to pitch in when needed (and back off when not) reshapes the nuclear family. In some households, for example, "mom" and "dad" are replaced with first names, emphasizing the camaraderie and, in a sense, leveling the playing field. This is not meant in disrespect, but rather, I have found, reflects a respectful acceptance and embrace of the changing relationship on par with close, steadfast peer-to-peer friendships.

I’m Still Here

Few things in life are black and white, and living together as grown-ups is no exception. It's not always easy or smooth sailing. And the desire for young adults in the U.S. to strike out on their own—sooner or later—holds for most.

Many, despite having an exit plan, be they in their 20s or 50s, who thought the arrangement would be temporary, say, “I’m still here.” They overcame rocky adjustment difficulties they initially encountered as children and stayed content in their refreshed nuclear family.

A friendship with parents isn’t what most returning home anticipate or expect. The research for Under One Roof Again was emphatic and explicit: There is no place like home for building and savoring these irreplaceable, lifelong friendships between adult children and parents, whether you stay longer than planned or set out on your own as soon as it’s feasible.
